title: Lucky

jokes.text: Leslie modeling interview outfits while Ben tries to go over talking points
jokes.setup: Ben is trying to conduct a serious pre-interview prep session with Leslie
jokes.punchline: Leslie keeps modeling clothes and says 'Keep going. I can still hear you.' — prioritizing fashion over substance
jokes.explanation: Classic Leslie/Ben dynamic — Leslie's chaotic energy vs. Ben's anxious professionalism. 'Keep going, I can still hear you' is a perfect Leslie line: cheerfully dismissive. Good character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Okay, I need to prepare for this interview. It's really important.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: That's great. You've got this.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Yeah, I'm just going to... wait, is this scarf working? Ben, look at this scarf. I'm thinking spring collection. Can you be the runway photographer?

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Leslie, weren't you just saying—

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Now I'm a hat model. This is a statement hat. Very controversial in the hat world.

jokes.text: 'And I bet they look even better on Ben's floor.'
jokes.setup: Ann and others are complimenting Leslie's new pants during a supposed professional prep session
jokes.punchline: Ann makes a sexually suggestive remark about Leslie's pants ending up on Ben's floor, hitting on Leslie on Ben's behalf
jokes.explanation: The economy of this joke is excellent — one line recontextualizes the entire fashion show moment as a flirtation. Ben's confused/mortified 'Are you hitting on Leslie... for me?' elevates it further.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: So what's this public works project about?

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Well, my pants are working for the public.

jokes.text: 'Are you hitting on Leslie... for me?'
jokes.setup: Ann just said Leslie's pants would look better on Ben's floor
jokes.punchline: Ben's baffled, almost touched reaction — parsing that Ann is acting as his romantic proxy
jokes.explanation: The comedic construction here is tight — the beat where Ben processes what Ann is doing and then can't decide if it's sweet or bizarre. The pause implied before 'for me?' is doing a lot of work. Very Ben.

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: Leslie, those pants look amazing on you.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Thanks! Ben said the same thing this morning.

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: Oh really? Where'd he see them?

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: On his bedroom floor.

jokes.text: It says 'Nympho' on the butt in silver, sparkly letters
jokes.setup: Leslie has been confidently modeling pants as a professional interview outfit
jokes.punchline: Someone notices the word 'Nympho' is written in bedazzled letters across the seat of the pants
jokes.explanation: The visual reveal lands hard. The sparkly letters detail makes it funnier — this isn't subtle. Works well as physical comedy conveyed through dialogue.

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: Leslie, you're so hot. I would totally do you.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Wait, what? Are you... are you flirting with Leslie on my behalf?

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: What? No! I'm just saying—

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Because I'm pretty sure that's not how this works.

jokes.text: 'Nympho means you're addicted to sex, and since it's on the butt, there's other implications as well. So those are a maybe.'
jokes.setup: Nympho pants have just been discovered as a potential interview outfit
jokes.punchline: Ben's clinical definition followed by 'other implications as well' and the hilariously diplomatic 'So those are a maybe' — treating this absurd situation with bureaucratic reasonableness
jokes.explanation: This is an exceptional Ben Wyatt joke. The comedy is entirely in his character: the earnest definition of nympho, the prim 'other implications as well' (refusing to say 'ass' out loud), and the devastating understatement of 'those are a maybe' treating butt-nympho pants as a borderline professional choice. Only Ben Wyatt says this. Very high rewatch value. Justifies the 8+ score.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Thank you all so much for the love on these pants. They're from a sustainable fabric company, and I got them on sale.

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: They're really flattering on you.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Yeah, those are fire.

dialogue.speaker: Jerry
dialogue.line: Very nice, Leslie.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Well, I'm glad everyone approves. I'm going to turn around now.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Leslie, wait—

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: What? I'm just turning—

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: Oh my God.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Whoa.

dialogue.speaker: Jerry
dialogue.line: My goodness.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: What? What is it?

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Your pants have a message on them.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: What message?

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: It says 'Treat yo' self, fool.'

jokes.text: Andy studying for his women's studies oral exam by reciting facts like a dog being trained with treats
jokes.setup: Andy is preparing for an oral exam in women's studies
jokes.punchline: He's being rewarded with literal dog treats for each correct answer — 'Treat, please.'
jokes.explanation: The image of Andy being trained like a dog to learn feminist theory is a great absurdist conceit. 'Treat, please' delivered earnestly by Andy is perfectly in-character — he has no self-awareness that this is undignified.

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: Well, technically, if you look at the medical definition, what we're talking about here is a clear violation of professional boundaries that could result in serious consequences including termination, legal action, and permanent damage to one's career and reputation.

jokes.text: 'Usually tests scare me, but this is an oral exam. And if there's one thing I know is—'
jokes.setup: Andy appears to be building to a double entendre about oral exams and oral sex
jokes.punchline: The scene cuts before he finishes, with the implication hanging in the air — then resumes with '— My fantastic— it's talk.'
jokes.explanation: The mid-sentence cut is a well-executed structural trick — the audience fills in the inappropriate answer themselves, then the show returns with Andy's innocent 'it's talk' deflation. Good editing comedy.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Wait, women's studies... that's just... studying women?

jokes.text: 'Told you — if you can't remember what some woman did, just tear up and say, She changed my life.'
jokes.setup: April is coaching Andy on how to handle his oral exam on feminist figures
jokes.punchline: Andy's cynical hack strategy: fake emotional vulnerability about a feminist figure you can't remember, delivered as if it's clever advice
jokes.explanation: Perfectly captures Andy's combination of laziness and accidental social manipulation. There's also a darkly subversive read — cynically weaponizing feminist sentiment. The economy is excellent: one sentence, clear setup, immediate laugh.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: I'm so nervous about this oral exam.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: I hope I don't mess up in front of everyone.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: I've been practicing my oral techniques all week.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: I really need to nail this oral performance.

jokes.text: Ben's reaction to meeting Buddy Wood: 'God, he is more tightly wound than ever. Maybe we should see if he can pull that rod out of his butt and we can hang some of those outfits on it.'
jokes.setup: Ben meets Buddy Wood, the high-strung morning show host, right before the crucial interview
jokes.punchline: Ben's talking-head suggestion to use Buddy's metaphorical butt rod as a coat rack — a rare moment of Ben being catty and snarky
jokes.explanation: The callback to the outfits ties it together neatly. Ben being unexpectedly cutting is funny because it's out of character. The image is vivid enough. Slightly overlong as a construction but works.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: I'm really good at coming... up with ideas.

jokes.text: Ann and Chris have gone 30 hours without breaking up; their personal best is 47 hours — which happened when Ann forgot they were dating while she was out of town
jokes.setup: Chris announces proudly that he and Ann have gone 30 hours without breaking up, framing it as an achievement
jokes.punchline: Their 'personal best' of 47 hours was because Ann forgot they were even dating — making the relationship even more pathetic than the 30-hour statistic implied
jokes.explanation: This is a masterclass in comedic escalation. The setup (30 hours without breaking up as an achievement) is already funny. Then 'our personal best is 47 hours' makes it worse. Then the kicker — she forgot they were dating — makes the relationship absurdly tragic. Three escalating jokes structured as one. Strong character integration: Chris's relentless positivity framing a disastrous relationship stat is very him.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: Just fake it. Pretend to care about stuff. It's not that hard.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: I've been doing it for years.

jokes.text: Ben and Ann discuss interview outfit with Ben suggesting 'No nonsense' and then Buddy Wood arrives
jokes.setup: Ben gives fashion advice about scarves and hats, landing on 'no nonsense' as the right energy
jokes.punchline: The word 'no nonsense' is immediately echoed by Leslie's confessional about the interview — good structural parallel, but the real payoff is the callback later when Leslie drunkenly says 'no-nonsense beverage'
jokes.explanation: Functions more as setup for a later callback than as a standalone joke. Gets rewatch bonus because 'no-nonsense' becomes a running gag. On its own, modest.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Ben is so tightly wound, if you straightened him out and used him as a rod, you could hang your entire winter coat collection on him.

jokes.text: 'Come on, did anyone even get hurt?' — Leslie's response to learning the interview is canceled due to a factory explosion
jokes.setup: The interview is canceled because Buddy has to return to Indianapolis for a factory explosion
jokes.punchline: Leslie's immediate, self-centered response — then immediately catching herself and apologizing
jokes.explanation: A great character joke — Leslie is good-hearted but her ambition occasionally makes her monstrous for a split second. The implied 'Sorry' beat after makes it work for a warm show. Short, sharp, character-specific.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: We're doing great! You know how long we've been together?

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: How long?

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Seven hours. That's a new record for us.

jokes.text: Ben's 'boring club' speech — the president is whoever lost the election for having the most boring speech; Ben implies Leslie might win
jokes.setup: Ben tells everyone to call it a night, suggesting they get an early start on door-to-door tomorrow
jokes.punchline: Tom snarks that they can 'make it back in time for boring club,' then Ben reveals the 'boring club' president lost an election because their speech was too boring — pointing at Leslie
jokes.explanation: A moderately funny exchange but the 'boring club' bit is a bit too convoluted and self-amused. The implication toward Leslie lands but the joke doesn't quite commit to the punchline cleanly.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Yeah, so we set this 47-hour record by just... not seeing each other.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Which, technically, means Ann forgot we were together.

jokes.text: Leslie: 'Ah, screw it. I got a new outfit. My hair looks amazing. And I have a serious excess of pre-interview adrenaline. Who's gonna drink with me?'
jokes.setup: Ben has been urging everyone to go home and prepare responsibly; Leslie seems to be following his lead
jokes.punchline: Leslie lists three completely self-absorbed reasons to go get drunk and immediately rallies everyone, undercutting her supposed professionalism
jokes.explanation: The three-item list works rhythmically and each item is funnier than the last ('excess of pre-interview adrenaline' is a great Leslie-ism). Strong character integration — Leslie's self-justifying logic for bad decisions is core to the character.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: This is terrible! A factory exploded and now my interview is cancelled!

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Wait, no. I mean, obviously the factory explosion is bad. But mostly I'm upset about my interview.

jokes.text: Chris: 'It happened when she was out of town for two days and she forgot we were dating.'
jokes.setup: Chris explains they achieved their 47-hour record
jokes.punchline: The record was only possible because Ann literally forgot they were in a relationship — making the 'achievement' even more pathetic
jokes.explanation: Beautiful escalation — takes the absurd premise of measuring a relationship in hours and adds a devastating kicker: the record only exists because Ann forgot about him. Brilliantly dark, economical, and specific. The understatement of Chris delivering this without any self-awareness makes it land harder.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Ben, you're president of the Boring Club.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Wait, what? There's a Boring Club?

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Yeah, and you won the election unanimously.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: I don't understand. I thought I was interesting.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: You were, until you lost. Turns out you're too boring even for the Boring Club. They had to create a new club just for you: the Even More Boring Club.

jokes.text: Andy's answer to 'what do you find cool about Susan B. Anthony' is... just restating that she was born in Adams, Massachusetts, in 1820
jokes.setup: The professor asks Andy for a 'freewheeling discussion' about what he got from the class; Andy has already stated the Adams, 1820 fact once
jokes.punchline: Andy's entire insight is to repeat the only fact he memorized, verbatim, and then add 'You know? Just one man's opinion.'
jokes.explanation: This is one of the episode's best jokes. The callback to the memorized fact from the study session, combined with the agonizing silence implied between 04:22 and 04:26, creates perfect build-up. 'Just one man's opinion' as a kicker to what is literally just a birth date and location is a brilliant Andy Dwyer line — he treats a meaningless fact as if it's a philosophical position. Earns the 8+ score for structure, character integration, and economy.

dialogue.speaker: Professor
dialogue.line: I'd like to open this up for a freewheeling discussion. Does anyone have any thoughts?

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Yeah, um... the raccoon is a marsupial.

jokes.text: Andy: 'I passed! I got a P!' then 'I was hoping for a P-plus, but that does not exist.'
jokes.setup: Andy passes his women's studies course on a pass/fail basis and celebrates
jokes.punchline: He expresses mild disappointment at not getting a P-plus — a grade that doesn't exist — as if he earned a near-miss on an impossible distinction
jokes.explanation: One of the funniest Andy Dwyer jokes in the episode. The idea that he'd be ambitious enough to want a P-plus but not understand it doesn't exist is perfectly calibrated to his character. The delivery implied here — genuine mild disappointment — makes it. Highly quotable. Earns 8+ for originality, character integration, and economy.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: I'm from Pawnee, Indiana.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: In my opinion.

jokes.text: 'Yes, so, basically, best grade in the class — tied for the best grade in the class.'
jokes.setup: Andy is bragging about his grade
jokes.punchline: He self-corrects mid-brag from 'best grade' to 'tied for best' — since everyone who passes gets a P, every passing student is tied for 'best'
jokes.explanation: The self-correction is a tight, well-structured joke. Andy's pride inflating to 'best grade' then immediately collapsing to 'tied for best' captures his irrepressible optimism without making him mean. Good economy.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: I got a C! That's like an A in Andy math!

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Wait, let me recalculate. Nope, still a C. I was hoping I'd discover a better grade if I did the math again.

jokes.text: Ron: 'Ron, I am a college graduate now.' / 'No, you're not.' / 'I'm a college course... Graduate'
jokes.setup: Andy triumphantly declares himself a college graduate to Ron
jokes.punchline: Ron's flat 'No, you're not' correction, and Andy's fumbling revision to 'college course graduate'
jokes.explanation: Ron's one-word-plus correction is perfectly in character — he won't let Andy have a factual inaccuracy even in a moment of celebration. The fumbled recovery 'college course... graduate' is sweet and funny. Good Ron/Andy interplay.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: I got an A! Wait, no, a B. But still the best grade in the class!

jokes.text: 'We'll let you pay for your own food, because of equality.'
jokes.setup: Andy invites the women's studies professor to join them for steak dinner
jokes.punchline: Ron's offer to 'let' the female professor pay her own way — framed as a feminist principle, but really Ron just doesn't want to pay for extra steak
jokes.explanation: This is a great Ron Swanson joke. He's invoking feminist egalitarianism as cover for his fiscal conservatism — a perfect character moment. The 'because of equality' tag is the comedic engine. Short, sharp, very Ron.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Professor, we're so glad you could come to dinner. We really believe in equality in this house.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: So that'll be $47.50 for your share of the meal.

jokes.text: Ann calls it a night saying she has a date with her bathtub, red wine, and 'a gigantic fireman named Marcus'
jokes.setup: The group is deciding whether to keep working or call it a night
jokes.punchline: Ann's self-care plan escalates from a bath and wine to a gigantic fireman named Marcus — making a joke out of both her romantic situation and her self-satisfaction
jokes.explanation: A solid quick joke. The escalation from relaxing bath to unnamed hookup is funny. 'Gigantic fireman named Marcus' is a good specific detail that implies a lot. The Marcus callback later adds bonus value.

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: I'm going home to read my romance novel tonight. My boyfriend Marcus is probably in there somewhere.

jokes.text: Ben talking-head with barely repressed anxiety, described as a 'strict mother' — 'It's like dealing with a strict mother who I am confusingly attracted to.'
jokes.setup: Leslie is venting in talking head about how the campaign has turned Ben from fun to stressed
jokes.punchline: 'It's like dealing with a strict mother who I am confusingly attracted to.'
jokes.explanation: An excellent Leslie talking-head joke. The 'strict mother' description of Ben is already funny; 'who I am confusingly attracted to' is the brilliant escalation that makes it a great joke about their relationship dynamic. Very quotable and character-specific.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: You should try drinking more milk. It's good for your bones.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: I've switched to an all-milk diet. I drink milk for breakfast, lunch, and dinner. I bathe in milk. I've replaced all the water in my house with milk.

jokes.text: 'Ben is like a MILF.'
jokes.setup: Leslie has just described Ben as a strict mother she's confusingly attracted to
jokes.punchline: Ann distills the entire description into 'Ben is like a MILF' — a perfectly vulgar and yet accurate summation
jokes.explanation: This is one of the episode's best jokes. It's a perfect callback-compression: Leslie gives a 20-word explanation of her feelings, Ann collapses it to three syllables that are both accurate and absurd. Maximum economy. High quotability. The joke also works because it reframes Ben (a male character) through a female-coded term without making it mean — it's weirdly affectionate. Justifies 8+ for economy and structure.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Ben's been so stressed lately about the budget cuts. He's been working non-stop, barely sleeping, and honestly it's kind of attractive.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Wait, is that weird? I think I'm confusing maternal attraction with actual attraction.

jokes.text: Ben calling Leslie while she's clearly drunk, claiming he's home watching Murder She Wrote — then repeating 'Murder She Wrote' as if convincing himself
jokes.setup: The interview is back on and Ben calls Leslie; she answers clearly intoxicated while pretending to be fine
jokes.punchline: Ben announces he's home watching Murder She Wrote — the most staid, unhip show imaginable — and then doubles down by repeating it, implying he's embarrassed by it
jokes.explanation: The Murder She Wrote detail is a nicely specific, character-appropriate embarrassment for Ben. The repeat ('Murder She Wrote. I'm watching Murder She Wrote.') implies self-conscious backpedaling. Mild but effective.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: You know what? I like that you're strict. I find it really attractive.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Really?

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Yeah. You're like a DILF.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: A what?

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Dad I'd Like to... you know.

jokes.text: 'We are so drucky. I mean lunky.'
jokes.setup: Leslie is trying to say they are 'drunk and lucky' as the interview gets reinstated
jokes.punchline: Her brain-scrambled portmanteau attempts — 'drucky' and 'lunky' — perfectly convey her intoxicated state while being endearing
jokes.explanation: A fun drunk-Leslie moment. The failed portmanteaus ('drucky,' 'lunky') work because they actually make phonetic sense as attempts — she's not just babbling. Character-specific to Leslie's compulsive word-coining habit.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I'm home! I'm home and I've been home. Home is where I am. I'm at home.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Leslie, where are you?

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I told you, I'm home! At my home! The home that is mine!

jokes.text: 'Both cabs in this town are busy' — Tom's solution is the remaining hours on the hot-tub limousine
jokes.setup: They need transportation to the airport immediately
jokes.punchline: Tom has both cabs accounted for ('both cabs in this town') and pivots to the hot-tub limo as the logical solution — treating absurd extravagance as pragmatism
jokes.explanation: 'Both cabs in this town' is a perfectly efficient Pawnee joke — the entire municipal poverty of the town communicated in four words. Tom using the hot-tub limo as practical transport is good Tom character comedy.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Oh my god, this is the best day ever! I'm so drunk— I mean, so lucky! Wait, no... so... drucky? Is that a word? I'm feeling very drucky right now!

jokes.text: Tom: 'I still had eight hours rental time on that hot-tub limousine I got for your campaign event, and it's on its way.'
jokes.setup: The cabs are unavailable; they need transportation to the airport urgently
jokes.punchline: Tom solves a serious campaign emergency with a hot-tub limousine — which he had already rented for a campaign event (of course he did)
jokes.explanation: Tom renting a hot-tub limousine for a city council campaign event is perfectly Tom. The casual delivery of 'I still had eight hours rental time' implies this is not the first time he's been in this situation.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: I got you covered. I got a hot-tub limo picking me up at 6 AM.

jokes.text: 'Diddly diddly diddly diddly swag.' / 'You did it right!' / 'I did it right.'
jokes.setup: Tom has just successfully arranged emergency transport via hot-tub limo
jokes.punchline: Tom's self-congratulatory gibberish ('diddly diddly diddly diddly swag') followed by seeking and receiving validation is a pure Tom Haverford character beat
jokes.explanation: Tom's self-congratulatory nonsense is in-character but the joke is more charming than hilarious. 'Diddly diddly diddly diddly swag' is committed absurdism from a character who speaks in made-up slang.

jokes.text: Drunk practice interview: 'Leslie, in your humble opinion... Why are you from Russia?' / 'I don't know.'
jokes.setup: Ann is trying to give Leslie a mock interview in the hot-tub limo to prepare for Buddy Wood
jokes.punchline: Ann's first practice question is completely incoherent ('Why are you from Russia?') and Leslie just accepts it and says 'I don't know' as if it's a fair question
jokes.explanation: A tight, absurdist drunk joke. The question is perfectly wrong — not just hard, but conceptually broken — and Leslie's defeated 'I don't know' treats it as a reasonable interview challenge she's failing. Good economy.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: My mother was a very powerful woman. She once heard a man say women shouldn't be allowed to vote, and she hit him so hard with a cast iron skillet that it bent the skillet.

jokes.text: Ron's talking-head: 'My father once told my mother that woman was made from the rib of Adam, and my mom broke his jaw.'
jokes.setup: Ron is being asked about his feminist credentials based on Andy's paper — the professor notes Andy called him a positive male role model
jokes.punchline: Ron's anecdote about his mother breaking his father's jaw for the rib-of-Adam comment — framed as evidence of powerful women shaping his life
jokes.explanation: This is the episode's single best joke. The setup — Ron claiming his life has been shaped by powerful women — sounds like a progressive statement. The punchline is dark, specific, physical, and entirely consistent with Ron's family mythology (established throughout the series). 'My mom broke his jaw' lands as both funny AND characterizes Ron's upbringing precisely. It's also a great feminist joke from a non-feminist character. Exceptional character integration — no one else on TV could deliver this line. Justifies 8.5+ across the board.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: Why are you eating alone?

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: I'm not alone. There are strangers here.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: That doesn't mean you're not eating alone.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: Strangers are just friends you haven't met yet.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: No they're not.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: Well, that's what my mom always said.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: Your mother was wrong.

jokes.text: April's book: 'the true story of a woman born with no arms and no legs who attempted to swim the English Channel' — 'That's impossible.' / 'Oh, she drowned immediately.'
jokes.setup: April is eating alone at the restaurant and tells Chris she's 'engrossed' in a book about a woman with no limbs who attempted to swim the English Channel
jokes.punchline: 'Oh, she drowned immediately. It's kind of a sad story.' Delivered with total April deadpan.
jokes.explanation: This is tied for the episode's best joke. The construction is perfect: Chris's earnest 'That's impossible' creates the straight-man setup. 'Oh, she drowned immediately' is a shocking, pitch-black punchline that lands the exact moment you process what it means. 'It's kind of a sad story' is the deadpan kicker that makes it even funnier by understating the horror. Totally April — she'd actually find this book cool. Maximum economy, high originality, perfect character integration.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: I wrote a book about my life. It's called 'Swanson: A Binary Search.' In it, I describe how I became Ron Swanson by eating nothing but breakfast meat and slowly losing all human emotion. By the end of the book, I've achieved my goal—I'm now Ron Swanson. The book ends with me sitting in my office, completely satisfied, having transcended humanity.

jokes.text: April to Chris: 'I'm not. I'm surrounded by friends... Friends I don't know yet.'
jokes.setup: Chris asks why April is eating alone
jokes.punchline: April claims she's surrounded by friends — then clarifies they're 'friends I don't know yet' — strangers she's redefined as potential friends to deflect pity
jokes.explanation: A solid April joke — her instinct to make something that could be sad (eating alone) into something that sounds philosophically cool. 'Friends I don't know yet' is a good line, though it's slightly warm for April's usual register.

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: I can't do the romance novel bath tonight. I have to go home and yell at my fictional boyfriend for two hours.

jokes.text: April to Chris after her dark book description: 'Cool.' [agreeing about the sad story]
jokes.setup: April describes a deeply morbid book.
jokes.punchline: Chris responds 'Cool' — a completely wrong emotional register, possibly being polite, possibly agreeing on the grimness.
jokes.explanation: A one-word reaction beat that shows Chris processing and filing away what he heard without knowing what to do with it. Works as a brief character moment in conjunction with joke 36.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie Knope
dialogue.line: I'm so heppy!

jokes.text: Ann cancels Marcus the fireman: 'I'm sorry, Marcus, I'm gonna have to cancel our bath. Something interesting is happening. I want to watch it. I don't know, Marcus. I'll hit you up when I hit you up.'
jokes.setup: Ann had announced plans to spend the night with Marcus; something more interesting has come up at the restaurant
jokes.punchline: Ann dismisses the gigantic fireman as casually as canceling a coffee order — 'I'll hit you up when I hit you up' has the breezy callousness of someone very comfortable with their romantic power
jokes.explanation: The callback to Marcus lands as a payoff joke. The casualness of 'I'll hit you up when I hit you up' is funny because it's how you'd text a peer, not dismiss a large fireman you'd planned to bathe with.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie Knope
dialogue.line: Pawnee is the greatest city in the world.

dialogue.speaker: Buddy
dialogue.line: Wait, you actually believe that?

dialogue.speaker: Leslie Knope
dialogue.line: Of course I do.

dialogue.speaker: Buddy
dialogue.line: Oh my God, she means it.

jokes.text: Leslie after the hot-tub limo ride to the airport: 'Wow, I feel totally normal. I'm ready to do this.'
jokes.setup: Leslie has just arrived at the airport after riding a hot-tub limousine while drunk, to do a major TV interview
jokes.punchline: Her complete self-conviction that she is fine — obviously belied by everything that has happened
jokes.explanation: A functional dramatic irony joke — the audience knows she isn't fine. Not the sharpest moment but it serves the escalating cringe structure of the interview setup.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie Knope
dialogue.line: We need to find a good spot for the interview at the airport.

dialogue.speaker: Ron Swanson
dialogue.line: The airport is so bad, they had to find a non-smelly spot just to conduct basic business.

jokes.text: Buddy Wood to Leslie: 'Oh. Oh, I'm sorry. You're being serious.' — about welcoming him to 'the greatest city in the world' (Pawnee)
jokes.setup: Leslie warmly welcomes Buddy Wood to 'the greatest city in the world'
jokes.punchline: Buddy visibly processes that she believes this, then condescendingly apologizes for assuming she was joking
jokes.explanation: Good character joke — Leslie's sincere civic pride versus Buddy's metropolitan condescension. The 'Oh. Oh, I'm sorry. You're being serious.' structure is a well-executed double take. Effective for establishing Buddy as an antagonist the audience immediately dislikes.

dialogue.speaker: Buddy
dialogue.line: Welcome to Pawnee, Indiana. Our main feature is toxic waste.

jokes.text: Leslie in drunk-speak: 'I think we more than make up for it with friendly faces and hand-working hards — hardworking hands.'
jokes.setup: Leslie is trying to defend Pawnee's charm in a live interview with Buddy Wood while drunk
jokes.punchline: She mangles 'hardworking hands' into 'hand-working hards' and then partially self-corrects — the drunk stumble over a cliché she's surely said a thousand times
jokes.explanation: The specific choice of 'hand-working hards' is perfectly drunk — it's not random, it's a plausible rearrangement. Leslie's own self-correction ('hardworking hands') shows she knows what she meant but can't quite get there. Strong character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Pawnee is the greatest city in the world! We have the most inspiring history, the most delicious food, and the most... most... *hiccups* ...the most adequate sidewalks!

jokes.text: Buddy Wood's narration: Pawnee is 'home to the Sweetums Candy Corporation, 19 toxic-waste repositories, and not much else'
jokes.setup: Buddy introduces Pawnee for his segment with the gravitas of a serious news reporter
jokes.punchline: The list of Pawnee's defining features — candy, 19 toxic waste sites, nothing else — delivered in serious documentary voice
jokes.explanation: The '19 toxic-waste repositories' is a terrific specific detail — specific enough to be absurd, large enough to be a defining feature. The straight-news delivery against the absurd content is well-executed. Economy is strong.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: Their offspring would be genetically perfect. They would dominate the human race.

jokes.text: Buddy pivots from Leslie's airport improvement pitch to declare it a 'metaphor' — 'Are you familiar with the term?'
jokes.setup: Leslie is making a sincere pitch about improving the airport and points to a specific worker as evidence
jokes.punchline: Buddy dismissively reframes the airport as a metaphor for Pawnee's worthlessness, then condescendingly checks whether Leslie knows what a metaphor is
jokes.explanation: Buddy's condescension explaining 'metaphor' to Leslie (who is clearly smart) is an effective character joke that builds audience resentment toward him. 'Are you familiar with the term?' is a good specific line.

dialogue.speaker: Chris
dialogue.line: Your deltoids are really well-defined.

jokes.text: 'If they got together, they would make the most beautiful super baby. It would rule us all. But what if super baby became too powerful? I guess we'll just have to take that chance.'
jokes.setup: April is observing Chris and Professor Linda meeting for the first time and finding them physically attractive as a pair
jokes.punchline: April's imagination spirals from 'cute couple' to genetically superior super baby to world domination — then accepts the risk as worth it
jokes.explanation: An exceptional April talking-head. The comedy escalates through three distinct beats: (1) cute couple, (2) world-dominating super baby, (3) accepting the risk of global subjugation for aesthetics. 'I guess we'll just have to take that chance' is a perfectly resigned, darkly logical kicker. This is pure April Ludgate logic — consequences are irrelevant if the aesthetic outcome is good. Earns 8+ across originality, structure, and character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I'm not going to talk about this. It's private and I'm not discussing it.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Actually, you know what? I slept with someone. It was amazing. We did it on a fur rug and I came so hard I saw colors I didn't know existed. I'm pretty sure I invented a new color.

jokes.text: April's cynical reason for wanting Chris and Linda together: 'if they get married, he'll spend all his time with her, and I might never have to talk to him again'
jokes.setup: April explains why she's invested in Chris getting a new girlfriend
jokes.punchline: She doesn't care about Chris's happiness — she's matchmaking purely for her own peace and quiet
jokes.explanation: April's self-interested 'generosity' is a perfect character joke. The reveal that her matchmaking is motivated by wanting to avoid Chris is a good subversion of the warm setup. Good economy.

dialogue.speaker: Buddy
dialogue.line: Are you drunk?

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: No, I'm not drunk. Alcohol causes drunkenness.

jokes.text: Chris and Ron competing to compliment Professor Linda's arms, with Ron invoking 'male gaze' concerns before asking to physically examine her lateral arm muscle
jokes.setup: Chris and Ron are both immediately struck by Professor Linda's physical fitness; Ron mentions the male gaze from women's studies context
jokes.punchline: Ron invokes 'male gaze' as an awareness concern, then immediately asks 'May I see?' — reaching to feel her arm muscle anyway, making the theory reference entirely performative
jokes.explanation: A great callback to the women's studies thread — Ron has absorbed exactly one concept (male gaze) and uses it to theoretically excuse what he's about to do anyway. The 'May I see?' after naming the concern is well-structured irony. Ron and Chris competing over a woman's arms is absurd but grounded in their characters.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I'm fine, I'm fine. It was just the microphone wire. These things are a hazard.

jokes.text: Ron orders a third steak mid-conversation about impressive arm muscles: 'Kendra? I am gonna have that third steak after all.'
jokes.setup: Ron is feeling physically inspired by the conversation about fitness and muscles
jokes.punchline: His response to being around athletic people is to immediately order a third steak
jokes.explanation: A perfect Ron Swanson joke — his response to admiring someone's athletic physique is to order more steak. Internally consistent with his entire value system. 'Third steak' implies he'd already had two, which is its own background joke. Great character integration.

jokes.text: Buddy confronts Leslie about her 'affaire de coeur' with Ben, translating it himself: 'affair of the heart'
jokes.setup: Buddy introduces the Ben topic with fancy French phrasing, apparently to seem sophisticated
jokes.punchline: He immediately translates it himself — 'affair of the heart' — deflating the affectation entirely
jokes.explanation: A small character joke about Buddy's self-satisfied pomposity. The self-translation undercuts his pretension. Mild; mainly functions to characterize Buddy.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Wait, Buddy, your metaphor doesn't make any sense. You can't use a sheep as a tiramisu. A sheep is a living animal, and tiramisu is a dessert. They're completely different things.

jokes.text: Leslie half-drunkenly starts to spill about her relationship with Ben before catching herself: 'I've had a couple drinks, so what the hell? Ben and I first—'
jokes.setup: Leslie has been deflecting Buddy's questions about Ben; the tequila erodes her discipline and she starts to confess on camera
jokes.punchline: She actually begins spilling before being interrupted by Buddy asking if she's inebriated — saving her from herself in the worst possible way
jokes.explanation: Good escalating cringe — the audience has been dreading this moment since they got in the hot-tub limo. The 'I've had a couple drinks, so what the hell?' surrender is a good Leslie line. The interruption before she fully incriminates herself is solid structure.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Wait, so you're telling me P-plus doesn't exist? But I got a P-plus on my last test!

dialogue.speaker: Teacher
dialogue.line: No, Andy. There's no P-plus. The lowest passing grade is a D.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: So what's the P stand for?

jokes.text: Buddy asks 'Ms. Knope, are you inebriated?' and Leslie responds 'What? No. Preposterous.' — then hiccups on camera
jokes.setup: Leslie is insisting she is not drunk on live television
jokes.punchline: Her denial is immediately punctuated by an on-camera hiccup — the most classic sitcom drunk tell, perfectly timed
jokes.explanation: The hiccup undercuts the denial perfectly; 'Preposterous' is a great Leslie word choice — it's more articulate than 'no' but still betrays anxiety. The joke is structurally sound but relies on a stock sitcom device (drunk person denies being drunk, then burps/hiccups). Originality docked accordingly.

dialogue.speaker: Professor
dialogue.line: A P-plus is impossible.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Actually, that's not true. In my women's studies class, we learned that nothing is impossible if you believe in yourself and you have the support of the people around you.

jokes.text: Buddy lists Leslie's drinks on camera: 'when you have a jumbo margarita and some flaming tequila shots, you can get drunk'
jokes.setup: Leslie has denied being drunk on camera; Buddy has clearly gathered intelligence on her evening
jokes.punchline: Buddy catalogs her specific drinks on the record, treating it as breaking news while Leslie helplessly watches her evening become a segment
jokes.explanation: A good cringe escalation moment. 'Jumbo margarita and some flaming tequila shots' as a broadcast news detail is funny. Serves the cringe structure more than being a standalone joke.

dialogue.speaker: Jerry
dialogue.line: I printed 500 flyers for the parks department, but I accidentally ordered them in the wrong size. They're too big to fit in any standard mailbox.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Jerry, how is that even possible?

dialogue.speaker: Jerry
dialogue.line: I don't know, I just... I clicked the wrong button.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: This is the most government thing I've ever heard of.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: We spent $2,000 on these.

dialogue.speaker: Jerry
dialogue.line: I'm sorry. I'm really sorry.

jokes.text: Leslie tries to end the interview and catches her mic wire: 'This is not because I'm drunk. This is because of the wire.'
jokes.setup: Leslie storms off the interview in humiliation but gets tangled in her microphone wire
jokes.punchline: She immediately offers a sober-sounding technical explanation for her stumble, further confirming she is drunk
jokes.explanation: The unprompted technical disclaimer is a perfect drunk move — nobody not drunk would need to specify 'it's not the drunk, it's the wire.' Character-specific (Leslie always has an explanation for everything) and well-timed. Good economy.

jokes.text: Buddy: 'A fitting end to a bizarre interview and a sad moment in a depressing city with no hope, in the waning moments of the bitter saga that has been a contentious campaign.'
jokes.setup: The interview has collapsed into chaos
jokes.punchline: Buddy delivers his sign-off in full melodramatic news anchor mode — 'depressing city with no hope' and 'bitter saga' as serious journalistic framing
jokes.explanation: Buddy's over-the-top journalistic framing of what is essentially a local council race is funny. The gap between the weight of language ('bitter saga,' 'waning moments') and the trivial subject is the joke.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: I'm offering each of you young people $5 to take care of your technology needs. A new computer, a phone, whatever you need.

dialogue.speaker: Young Person
dialogue.line: Um, that's not going to cover much.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: Not cover much? In my day, $5 could buy you a house and a car. What's changed?

jokes.text: 'The sheep that watch my show are gonna eat this up like tiramisu.' / 'Tiramisu is an Italian dessert often—' / 'I know what tiramisu is, okay? And sheep don't eat it.'
jokes.setup: Buddy says his viewers will 'eat this up like tiramisu'; Leslie starts to define tiramisu
jokes.punchline: Buddy snaps that he knows what tiramisu is — 'And sheep don't eat it' — a correction that reveals he's also aware his own metaphor was mixed
jokes.explanation: A beautifully constructed joke. The comedy has two levels: (1) Leslie's compulsive factual correction in a crisis is perfectly in-character, (2) 'sheep don't eat tiramisu' is Buddy correcting his own mixed metaphor — he used sheep as an insult for his audience and then accidentally mixed it with a fancy Italian dessert. Both characters are funny here for opposite reasons. High quotability and rewatch value.

dialogue.speaker: Chris
dialogue.line: That's a... that's a really nice shirt, Ron. Is that a new shirt? Because it's very... blue.

jokes.text: Leslie: 'Tiramisu is an Italian dessert often—' Buddy: 'I know what tiramisu is, okay? And sheep don't eat it.'
jokes.setup: Buddy uses 'tiramisu' as a metaphor; Leslie begins explaining what it is
jokes.punchline: Buddy shuts down her explanation, then self-refutes his own metaphor ('sheep don't eat it') — catching himself in a bad mixed metaphor
jokes.explanation: This is a very clever joke. Leslie's instinct to explain 'tiramisu' (at her most Leslie, compulsively informative even in crisis) is undercut by Buddy claiming he already knows — but then Buddy immediately reveals a flaw in his own metaphor with 'and sheep don't eat it.' It collapses his intimidating moment into self-refutation. Great structure, good economy, and both characters are perfectly themselves.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: You know what? You need to learn to delegate more. That's what a real leader does.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: Where are you getting this?

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: You told me that!

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: I would never use the word 'leader' in that context.

jokes.text: 'Tomorrow morning this gets broadcast around the entire Indiana-sphere.'
jokes.setup: Buddy is threatening to air the disastrous interview footage
jokes.punchline: 'Indiana-sphere' — a pompous portmanteau that implies Buddy thinks Indiana is a media empire comparable to a 'biosphere'
jokes.explanation: A fun Buddy character detail — his inflated self-importance extends to the reach of his broadcast market. 'Indiana-sphere' is a good invented word that reveals his delusion. Quick, efficient.

dialogue.speaker: Chris
dialogue.line: Look, I'm fine with the whole Linda situation. I mean, it's not ideal, but I'm a mature adult who can handle—

dialogue.speaker: Chris
dialogue.line: Actually, you know what? I'm incredibly lonely and I miss having someone to talk to.

jokes.text: Andy's post-exam toast: 'Thank you for celebrating the most ultimate triumph of my life. I'm very proud of me, and you are too.'
jokes.setup: Andy is toasting the group at the celebratory dinner after passing his women's studies exam
jokes.punchline: 'I'm very proud of me, and you are too.' — Andy projecting his own pride onto everyone else as if it's a known fact
jokes.explanation: An excellent Andy line. 'I'm very proud of me' is already funny (the reflexive self-pride), but 'and you are too' is the kicker — he's decided everyone is proud of him and announces it as established fact. 'Most ultimate triumph' is also perfect Andy superlative-stacking. Very quotable, strong character integration. Just shy of 8 on craft — the structure is simple but efficient.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: April and I have been together for a whole month! That's like, a new record for us.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: We broke up twice last week.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Yeah, but we got back together both times! That's growth, April. That's what they call growth.

jokes.text: Andy to the professor: 'I'm taking your class again next semester. And I'm gonna lock down that P-plus.' / 'It's impossible.' / 'You and the women taught me that nothing is impossible.'
jokes.setup: Andy is thanking the professor and announces his intention to retake the class to get the P-plus
jokes.punchline: The professor says a P-plus is impossible; Andy turns this into an inspirational feminist lesson — 'you and the women taught me that nothing is impossible'
jokes.explanation: A very strong joke. The callback to P-plus is already good. The punchline — Andy using women's studies logic to insist on the existence of a nonexistent grade — is both absurd and structurally tight. 'You and the women' is a wonderfully clunky way to refer to feminist figures, and it works because Andy means it sincerely. Earns 8+ for structure, character integration, and the elegance of the callback payoff.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Happy anniversary! I got you condoms.

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: Why would you give me condoms?

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Well, we've been together for a year, right? And condoms come in boxes of 12. So I figured, you know, 12 times a year, that's once a month. And I want to have sex with you once a month.

jokes.text: Professor Linda mentions she teaches a morning Zumba class for retirees — immediately before Chris asks her out on a land kayaking date
jokes.setup: Professor Linda is leaving the dinner
jokes.punchline: The mundane detail of the retiree Zumba class followed immediately by Chris's absurdly specific date proposition ('land kayaking') lands as a joke about how earnest these two characters are
jokes.explanation: Two small jokes packaged together. The Zumba detail humanizes the professor unexpectedly; land kayaking is a perfectly Chris activity. Neither is exceptional but they function as mild character jokes.

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: Andy, what is this?

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: It's a gift! Do you like it?

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: It's a onesie with your face on it.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Yeah! So you can wear me all the time!

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: We're breaking up.

jokes.text: Ron and Professor Linda immediately agree to go home together after she says she isn't ready to date: 'Or how about you and I go back to my place?' / 'Yes.'
jokes.setup: Professor Linda has just told Chris she needs more time before jumping into anything; Ron has been a background presence during this conversation
jokes.punchline: Ron immediately propositions her; she immediately says yes — the 'not ready for a relationship' was specifically about Chris, and the quick-cut implication is that Ron is different
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best-constructed jokes. The setup appears to be about Chris's rejection, which is sweet and melancholy. Then Ron immediately undercuts it with a blunt proposition, and the professor's flat 'Yes' is the perfect punchline — no hesitation. The misdirection is excellent: we thought the scene was about Chris's pathos, and it becomes a Ron conquest joke. The economy is outstanding — four words for the punchline. Earns 8+ across the board.

jokes.text: The immediate cut to 'Wow!' after Ron and the professor leave together — implied reaction beat
jokes.setup: Ron has just successfully propositioned the professor Chris was trying to date
jokes.punchline: The stunned 'Wow!' from the table — and the implication that Chris is processing this in real time
jokes.explanation: The reaction beat extends the joke. The 'Wow!' adds a communal acknowledgment of what just happened and extends the audience's laughter from joke #52. Functional but not a standalone joke.

jokes.text: Ben declares 'Fun Ben lives' when he decides to get in the hot-tub limo
jokes.setup: After the nightmare interview, the crisis is over; Ben lets go of his campaign anxiety
jokes.punchline: 'Fun Ben lives' — Ben's self-naming of his relaxed alter ego as if he has to formally reinstate it
jokes.explanation: A fun character moment. The implication that Ben has to formally name and announce his own fun side is self-aware and slightly pathetic in the best way. 'Fun Ben' becoming a proper noun is good.

jokes.text: Leslie confesses her arson idea is sweet: 'Ah, it gets old.' Ben responds with weary familiarity
jokes.setup: Leslie says it's sweet that Ben threatened to commit arson for her; Ben says 'ah, it gets old'
jokes.punchline: Ben treats arson threats as a routine part of his life — the breezy 'it gets old' implies he has threatened arson many times
jokes.explanation: A tight Ben/Leslie joke. The 'it gets old' casualness about arson threats is a good deadpan. Character-appropriate for a couple where Leslie's chaotic ambition constantly pulls Ben into schemes.

jokes.text: Hot-tub limo driver: 'You know, no one ever used this hot-tub limo for actual transportation. And I can't take this thing on the highway, so it'll take a few extra hours.' / 'Hey, is this a seven or a one?'
jokes.setup: They've piled into the hot-tub limo to rush to Indianapolis
jokes.punchline: The driver reveals (1) this has never been used for actual transport, (2) it can't go on the highway, adding hours to the trip — then asks if an address digit is a 7 or a 1, implying he has no idea where he's going
jokes.explanation: Three layers of incompetence revealed in rapid succession — wrong vehicle, wrong route capability, can't read the address. The escalation from bad to worse is well-paced. The '7 or a 1?' kicker is strong.

jokes.text: Hot-tub limo driver squints at the GPS address and asks: 'Hey, is this a seven or a one?'
jokes.setup: The group has just committed to traveling to Indianapolis in a hot-tub limo that can't go on highways
jokes.punchline: The driver can't read the address clearly — adding another layer of incompetence to the already doomed plan
jokes.explanation: The escalating incompetence of the hot-tub limo plan gets one more beat. Simple but effective.

jokes.text: Jerry is still working at 4 AM — and has put the wrong flyers in the wrong envelopes for the entire night
jokes.setup: Jerry has been working through the night while everyone else went out; Ben checks in
jokes.punchline: Jerry reveals he's spent hours putting the wrong flyers in the wrong envelopes — he switched the handout flyers and the mailing flyers — and has to redo everything
jokes.explanation: A perfect Jerry joke — he stayed late to help and managed to waste the entire night doing it backwards. The patient, tired way he realizes it ('Oh, jeez. Oh, no.') is good physical/vocal comedy implied by the text.

jokes.text: 'Well, you know, it's like I always say. It ain't government work if you don't have to do it twice.'
jokes.setup: Jerry has just realized he's done all the campaign envelope work wrong and has to redo it
jokes.punchline: Jerry's cheerful folk wisdom about government inefficiency — applied to his own mistake as if the universe intended it this way
jokes.explanation: A good Jerry joke — he's so used to his own failures that he has a folk saying ready for this exact situation. 'It ain't government work if you don't have to do it twice' is a solid invented aphorism. The fact that Jerry says 'it's like I always say' implies this happens to him constantly.

jokes.text: 'I can't destroy the tape because I don't have it, because your sad, tiny backwater airport lost my bags.'
jokes.setup: Leslie has begged Buddy to destroy the tape of the disastrous interview
jokes.punchline: The tape is gone — not because Buddy is kind, but because the Pawnee airport (which Leslie was defending moments ago) lost his luggage
jokes.explanation: A beautifully ironic resolution. The airport that Leslie passionately defended in the interview is the instrument of her salvation — and Buddy has to deliver this in the most condescending way possible. The callback makes it structurally satisfying. 'Sad, tiny backwater airport' is good Buddy-speak.

jokes.text: 'You'd think a commuter airport could handle the luggage of 11 people at once, but apparently not.'
jokes.setup: Buddy is explaining how the airport lost the tape
jokes.punchline: The Pawnee airport is so small that handling 11 passengers' luggage simultaneously exceeds its capacity
jokes.explanation: A solid Pawnee smallness joke. 11 passengers as the breaking point is a good specific number — small enough to be absurd but specific enough to feel researched.

jokes.text: 'Thank God for that mitten factory tragedy.' — Buddy's cheerful gratitude for his other news story
jokes.setup: Buddy is consoled that even without the Leslie story, he has another big segment from Indiana
jokes.punchline: He thanks God for a factory tragedy — treating a presumably deadly industrial accident as a professional windfall, with complete sincerity
jokes.explanation: A sharp dark joke about media opportunism. 'Mitten factory tragedy' is a wonderfully specific Indiana detail, and the 'thank God' phrasing makes Buddy's callousness complete. The word 'mitten' does a lot of comedy heavy lifting — it's so humble and midwestern that a tragedy involving it sounds absurd. Strong economy.

jokes.text: Ron at the office the next morning: 'April, Andrew... Good morning to you both. Doughnuts — go nuts.'
jokes.setup: Ron arrives at work the morning after spending the night with Professor Linda
jokes.punchline: Ron's conspicuously good mood is expressed entirely through (1) the 'go nuts' doughnut pun delivered with zero acknowledgment that it's a pun, and (2) the fact that Ron, who rarely brings treats, brought doughnuts
jokes.explanation: This is one of the episode's best jokes and a great Ron Swanson character moment. The comedy has multiple layers: (1) Ron is in an inexplicably great mood the morning after secretly sleeping with the professor; (2) 'go nuts' is an uncharacteristic pun from a man who doesn't make puns; (3) Ron doesn't explain anything. The understatement is total — he expresses his entire post-coital bliss through doughnuts and a pun. Exceptional character integration. Earns 8+ easily.

jokes.text: Ron offers Andy and April money: 'Hey, you kids need any money? No? Go buy yourself a Walkman. How much is a Walkman nowadays? Probably more than $20. Here's $25.'
jokes.setup: Ron is in a generously good mood and offers money to Andy and April
jokes.punchline: He suggests they buy a Walkman (decades-obsolete technology), estimates the price, and gives them $25 — a generous impulse executed with completely outdated cultural reference
jokes.explanation: A great extension of Ron's good mood joke (#63). The Walkman detail is perfect — Ron is so disconnected from contemporary consumer technology that his reference gift is completely obsolete, and he does the math on it with complete confidence. '$25' as the final number after genuine deliberation is a good button. Highly quotable, strong character integration.

jokes.text: Andy uses Ron's own advice against him: 'You know, Ron, someone once told me this is not how grown-ups deal with tough situations. We face them head-on.' — a callback to Ron's earlier advice to Andy
jokes.setup: Andy is urging Ron to tell Chris; Ron is resisting
jokes.punchline: Andy quotes Ron's own advice back at him — the exact words Ron used to stop Andy from faking sick to avoid his oral exam
jokes.explanation: A well-structured callback that enriches both scenes retroactively. Andy using Ron's words against Ron is emotionally satisfying and funny — especially because Andy has to be the one teaching Ron the lesson. Ron's reaction ('Fine') and the awkward pause after make it even better. Earns high marks for structure and the earned payoff.

jokes.text: Ron's pause and then: 'Fine.' followed by the awkward silence before he goes to tell Chris
jokes.setup: Andy has successfully used Ron's own words against him and Ron has no counter-argument
jokes.punchline: Ron's clipped, defeated 'Fine.' followed by a beat where he processes having been outmaneuvered by Andy Dwyer
jokes.explanation: Maximum economy — 'Fine.' is one word that communicates Ron's complete defeat. The humor is in the reaction beat: Ron, the most stubborn man in Pawnee, being cornered by Andy and having no escape. The implied look-to-camera reaction is very funny on rewatch.

jokes.text: Ron's confessional about telling Chris: 'Fine.' — then the beat of Ron walking over to do it
jokes.setup: April has cornered Ron with his own logic and he must now tell Chris what happened
jokes.punchline: Ron's single word 'Fine.' and the implied begrudging walk-of-shame to tell Chris is the punchline — the most Ron response possible
jokes.explanation: Ron's single-word capitulation is peak economy. The joke is in what ISN'T said — Ron accepts the argument with complete brevity and moves on. Very Ron.

jokes.text: Andy: 'Oh, my God, Ron... It was you who told me that. That's crazy.'
jokes.setup: Andy has just quoted Ron's advice back at him, and it worked
jokes.punchline: Andy then apparently just NOW realizes who told him that — expressing genuine amazement at his own callback, as if he didn't plan to use it tactically
jokes.explanation: This is a great Andy moment — the implication is that Andy didn't strategically invoke Ron's words; he genuinely just thought of good advice and it happened to be Ron's words. He only puts it together AFTER it worked. 'That's crazy' as sincere amazement is perfect Andy. Strong character integration.

jokes.text: 'There's that shirt.' — April noticing Ron's red shirt again
jokes.setup: Ron is about to go tell Chris the news; April observes his conspicuous good mood and appearance
jokes.punchline: 'There's that shirt.' — April cryptically acknowledging that the red shirt is significant, implying she already knows Ron got lucky
jokes.explanation: Maximum economy again — three words that communicate April has fully deduced what Ron did last night. 'There's that shirt' is perfectly cryptic April-speak. The callback to Chris's oblivious compliment on the same shirt adds layers.

jokes.text: Ron tells Chris: 'After the bar last night, I... engaged in consensual activities with Linda.'
jokes.setup: Ron is doing the right thing and telling Chris he slept with Professor Linda
jokes.punchline: 'Engaged in consensual activities' — Ron's legalistic, clinical euphemism for sex, which is both more formal and more awkward than just saying it
jokes.explanation: An exceptional Ron Swanson line. 'Engaged in consensual activities with Linda' is the least romantic, most bureaucratically correct way to announce a sexual conquest. It's funny on multiple levels: (1) the legalistic phrasing ('consensual activities') is Ron's discomfort with emotional disclosure finding cover in procedural language, (2) 'with Linda' tacked on as if filing a form. Highly quotable, perfect character integration. One of the episode's top three jokes. Earns 8.5+ confidently.

jokes.text: Chris processes the news and responds: 'You're a good man, Ron.' — with sincere grace
jokes.setup: Ron has just told Chris he slept with the woman Chris was pursuing
jokes.punchline: Chris's response is the most magnanimous, emotionally evolved possible reaction — 'You're a good man, Ron' — which is both funny because it's sincere and because it makes Ron briefly look actually bad for what he did
jokes.explanation: A beautifully ironic character joke. Chris's relentless positivity means he congratulates Ron for telling him rather than condemning Ron for what he did. The comedy is in the gap between what would be a normal reaction (anger, hurt) and Chris's evolved response. Makes Chris sympathetic and funny simultaneously.

jokes.text: Chris in talking head: 'I'm quite lonely.' / then 'Ah, [bleep].'
jokes.setup: Chris has just processed that Ron slept with the woman he was interested in
jokes.punchline: His talking-head confession reduces his entire emotional state to 'I'm quite lonely' — then the bleep implies a stronger reaction follows
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's most effective emotional-comedy beats. 'I'm quite lonely.' is devastating and funny simultaneously — Chris's trademark understatement applied to genuine sadness. Then 'Ah, [bleep]' shatters his composure in a way that makes his earlier grace (joke #71) even funnier retroactively. The pairing of the two beats is excellent structure.

jokes.text: Ann and Tom's 48-hour anniversary gift: 48 condoms 'different flavor for each hour'
jokes.setup: Tom announces he and Ann have set a new personal record (48 hours without breaking up) and produces a gift
jokes.punchline: The gift is 48 condoms — one for each hour — in different flavors, presented with complete sincerity as a romantic gesture
jokes.explanation: A very strong callback payoff. The 48-condom gift is a great Tom Haverford joke: romantic in his mind, absurd in execution, impractical as a concept. 'Different flavor for each hour' implies he calculated this thoughtfully. Ann's immediate 'We're not dating anymore. Get out.' is the perfect button. Earns high marks for the callback structure and Tom character integration.

jokes.text: Ann: 'Yeah, we're not dating anymore, okay? Get out.' Tom: 'No, wait— Don't punish me. I took a risk.' Ann: 'Yeah. Bye.'
jokes.setup: Tom's 48-condom anniversary gift has not been received well
jokes.punchline: Tom's wounded 'Don't punish me. I took a risk.' treats a catastrophically misjudged gift as an act of romantic bravery deserving protection
jokes.explanation: 'Don't punish me, I took a risk' is a good Tom line — his self-perception as a bold romantic is completely divorced from reality. Ann's flat 'Yeah. Bye.' is the perfect dismissal. Good button to the episode's final joke sequence.

tmdb_overview: Leslie and Ben are thrilled when Buddy Wood wants to interview Leslie for his Indianapolis talkshow. April and Ron prep Andy for his final exam in his Women's Studies course.
insight: Mid-tier absurdist romp: 55 jokes in 26 minutes, but cringe-heavy humor undercuts the momentum.
